Investors Seek Safety in a Rocky Market
 
Plus, CoreWeave stock turns upward, and a tax-saving strategy is supercharging margin loans
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
JASON HENRY FOR WSJ
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Treasury yields fell as investors sought safety. Jitters about the AI trade pushed 10-year Treasury note yields to 5.09%. The decline of about a 10th of a percentage point was the largest in a day since August of last year. Other assets perceived as safe also rose. Gold prices were up 1.5%, and the Health Care Select Sector index rose 1.8%.

 

CoreWeave rose. It has been a wild couple of days for the AI cloud-computing player. The company’s shares fell more than 15% on Wednesday and fell further on Thursday morning, after a hot inflation reading led to concerns about interest-rate increases that would raise the company’s borrowing costs. But supportive comments from Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, whose company owns a big stake in CoreWeave, helped reverse the slide. CoreWeave ended the session up 5.9%.

 

Stocks rose. Shares recovered after a down session, led by a 1.1% gain for the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The Nasdaq rose 0.1%, and the S&P 500 was up 0.3%.

 

Producer prices came in hot. A 6.3% rise in wholesale prices from a year earlier in September was the highest reading in more than four years, adding to recent data suggesting inflation is reverberating through the U.S. economy. Combined with the 3.7% reading for consumer-price inflation in September, the wholesale price inflation bolsters the case for higher rates when the Fed’s policy-setting body meets in two weeks.

One Big Story

 
 
JUTHARAT PINYODOONYACHET FOR WSJ
 

A wildly popular tax-saving strategy is pushing borrowing for stock trading to the limit. Margin-loan balances on Charles Schwab’s books nearly doubled in the third quarter to about $188 billion, largely because of the tax strategy. The trade has been so popular that Schwab has restricted clients using it, as it entails taking significant balance-sheet risk. Under the strategy, investors go long on stocks but also bet against them, generating returns but at the same time creating losses that reduce tax liability.
